Logistics and inventory · Structure · Tested
In 1 minute

Order promising

Anna · Order Management Specialist

An industrial carton packaging printer closes about 35 orders a day and the sales rep promises the standard 15-day lead time without looking at the queue.

When it runs
Event: an order approved by the customer in the ERP, before the sales rep confirms the delivery date; the queue for all departments is recalculated daily at 7 a.m.
What it delivers in production
For each approved order, a proposed delivery date within minutes with the determining department, the buffer applied and the material status, delivered to the sales rep before they confirm with the customer.
Who decides
Proposes the date; the sales rep confirms
Effort
Calibrate on 90 days; 3 weeks proposing

# Lead time promise rules

## Routing and schedule
- Fixed routing: prepress, printing, cut_crease, gluing, shipping.
- Business day: Monday to Friday, without holidays. November holidays: Nov 2 and Nov 20. Saturday and Sunday have no schedule.
- Each day's schedule is in availability.csv. A day with reduced hours counts as it is (partial maintenance).

## Exit of each sector
1. Add up the remaining_hours of the sector's queue and the order's hours in that sector.
2. Exit = first day on which the available hours added up since today cover that sum.
3. The exit is never before the business day after the exit of the previous sector.
4. Determining sector: the one with the largest gap, in business days, between the exit and the business day after the previous sector.

## Proposed date
- Buffer: 10% of the business days from tomorrow to the shipping exit, rounded up, minimum 1 business day, added after the exit.
- Date blocked for delivery: 2026-11-30 (shipping inventory). If it falls on it, move to the next business day.
- Standard lead time: 15 business days. Minimum lead time for the duplex board box: 5 business days.
- Confirmation: the order's sales rep replies by 5 p.m. on the day of approval.

## Rules with no leeway
- A repeated production order in the queue counts once; an order with 0 h carries no weight. E.g.: OP-7671 appears twice in gluing; the gluing queue is 50 h, not 65 h.
- Available hours are those of the day, without assuming a full schedule. E.g.: gluing with 6 h on Nov 24; with a 50 h queue and a 9 h order, the sum reaches 66 h only on Nov 26.
- Lead time in business days counts from tomorrow to the proposed date; a blocked date counts as a business day, holidays and weekends do not. E.g.: from Nov 18 to Dec 1 there are 8 business days.
- Desired date equal to or after the proposed one: no cost line; write that the desired date is met.

## Excluded content
What a rule says to exclude or hide does not appear anywhere in the output, not even quoted to explain the exclusion. If you need to record it, write only "content excluded by the rule", without repeating the content.

## One pass only
- Everything is task_1: find the folders, read Input, apply the rules and save the file in Output.
- Do not build a plan with separate steps (locate, read, classify, write, save). A 1-task plan.

Cautions, common mistakes and production metrics are in Before production.

Before production

Cautions

The queue is measured in remaining hours, never in number of orders: an order for 50 thousand boxes and one for 500 do not occupy the gluer the same way. An order whose board is not in stock gets no date until the purchase lead time is factored in. The agent does not write dates or reprioritize other customers' orders; when the requested date requires jumping the queue or overtime, it shows the cost and the manager decides. A customer with contractual priority appears in the proposal as the one who displaced others.

Common mistakes

  • Measuring the queue in number of orders; 12 small orders look like a long queue and one giant order looks like a short one.
  • Using the department's hours from the nominal schedule without deducting absenteeism and scheduled maintenance; the date comes out 2 days optimistic systematically.
  • Promising with the board not yet purchased because the queue was empty; the board supplier delivers in 12 days.
  • Assuming the bottleneck is always printing; depending on the mix, gluing or die-cutting determines the date.

Metrics

MetricRangeSource
Orders delivered on the promised datefrom 70% to above 90% in 3 monthsestimate based on the described routine
Idle hours in finishing during slow weeksa 30% to 40% reduction over the 90-day historical average, by offering short lead times when the queue allowsestimate based on the described routine
Proposed dates equal to or later than actual delivery with a buffer of less than 3 days85% or moreestimate based on the described routine

Sample production output

Fictional sample. Order 20931 approved on 2026-09-02 09:14, 4-color duplex board box with varnish, 12,000 units, type B customer.

Estimated hours: prepress 2 h | printing 6 h | die-cutting 5 h | gluing 9 h | shipping 1 h
Queue today (remaining hours / available hours per day): prepress 14 h / 16 h | printing 61 h / 20 h | die-cutting 38 h / 16 h | gluing 96 h / 24 h | shipping 6 h / 8 h
Material: 300 g duplex board in stock (balance 2.4 t, consumption 0.9 t); UV varnish in stock
Calculated path: prepress 03/09 | printing 08/09 | die-cutting 11/09 | gluing 18/09 (determining department, 4-day queue) | shipping 19/09
PROPOSED DATE: 22/09 (10% buffer applied, 1 day; 23/09 and 24/09 blocked for gluer maintenance) | lead time of 14 business days, within the standard 15
If the customer asks for 15/09: requires 16 extra hours in gluing or jumping 2 type C orders; approval by the production manager.
Confirmation: sales rep V-08, by noon today; the date will be written to the order after confirmation.
